chapter: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
title: Fletcher too easy-going: the band arrives late at Fall River
summary: On a Massachusetts one-nighter with men driving their own cars, only Fletcher and Horace were present at 8:40. Hawkins, the drummer and John Kirby (lost) straggled in, and Fletcher never reprimanded them.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: How was Fletcher to work for? Was he easy going or was he, again, pretty --

Oh, he was too easy a lot of times. You know, I can cite an instance in -- actually one time when I was playing with Fletcher's band, we were playing a series of one nighters up in Massachusetts, and this was when Fletcher's band was traveling by individual automobiles instead of a bus. And we had guys in the band like John Kirby, Coleman Hawkins, Louis Armstrong, Kaiser Marshall, Elmer Chambers and guys like that during that era, you know.

And they all had individual cars, and all Fletcher would tell them when they left New York, "We're playing up in Fall River, Massachusetts. It's on highway so and so.. We hit at 9:00 o'clock, and we're wearing such and such a thing." And he'd tell them this the night before. Okay, we don't see the guys no more.

Well, I remember one time Fletcher was driving his Packard, it was one of those old long roadsters, funny things, Maine, and I was riding with him, and he always kept his books in the -- there's a compartment on the side where he could put six on one side, and they'd just fit. Six on the other.
Yeah, I remember those. Yes, I do.
Anyway, this is where he used to carry them. Of course, the boys in the band carried their own horns. So I remember one time we were playing up in

Massachusetts, and it was 20 minutes of 9:00. There was nobody in the house, as far as the band was concerned, except Fletcher and myself. And he seemed just as unconcerned about, you know -- me, I was worrying to death.

I went outside and was trying to look down the highway to see if I could see anybody, you know. I'd go back in and Fletcher's sitting at the piano just fooling around, playing. This is honest, the truth; this has happened more than once. And I was -- man, I was worrying so much, I was -- I should have been in bad health, you know, from worrying. But anyway, he never worried, and the guy didn't bother him, so -- well, about quarter of 9:00 here comes Coleman Hawkins in. About ten minutes of 9:00 here comes the drummer, ten minutes of 9:00 -- the drummer!

To set up -- John Kirby was such an erratic roadsign reader that he went through the town which that we were going to play in and went 15 miles on the other side. And he asked somebody, 'What direction is Fall River?' They said, 'Back down the highway here the way you just came, 15 miles,' and all this thing, so he got in about 9:20, the bass player, so it happened that about 9:45 we had a full band, and the people were coming in, you know.
And Fletcher would start off with four or five musicians, man, and it worried me to death.

We talked to the promoter that was running the affair, and he told them maybe they had a flat or something, you know, one of those things, you know. Finally, about 10:00 o'clock we had a full band. And the guys played after they got there so hard, you know the guys in some instances didn't cut any money off the contract. They honored the full contract because the house was full, and they always played a little bit overtime.

But when they got there, they played, but man -- it was -- oh, man, you were on edge. Not Fletcher! He didn't worry. And he never reprimanded the guys for it, you know. They were easy going, but they would seem as if they would play harder, you know. He was too easy on them. But I've often heard him say, 'Well, you don't ride your musicians,' you know. 'You tell them what you want done. If they don't do it, then you try to look for a capable replacement, if you can find one.' This was his answer.

So this was his pattern. Everybody knows Smack is an easy going guy, and the greatest harm he ever did to anybody was to himself by being too easy with these guys. But anytime he had a battle of musical jazz,
